lead: BQP is the set of yes-or-no problems that a quantum computer can settle in polynomial time with small error. It is the honest yardstick for what quantum hardware can do fast. Shor's algorithm puts integer factoring inside BQP, so quantum machines beat the best known classical methods there. But nobody has placed an NP-complete problem inside BQP. This chapter defines the class, draws the inclusions that are proved, and explains why Grover's quadratic speedup does not turn an exponential search into a polynomial one.
prereq: You need: Shor's factoring algorithm, Grover's search, and the big-O notation from Unit 1 (Foundations).

sections.h3: P, NP and BQP in plain terms

blocks.text: A complexity class is a set of decision problems, that is, problems whose answer is yes or no. Problems are grouped by the resources needed to solve them. The resource here is time, counted as a function of the input length n, which is the number of input bits.
P holds every problem that a classical deterministic computer can settle in time O(nk) for some fixed k. Adding two n-bit numbers is in P.

NP holds every problem whose YES answer can be checked in polynomial time from a short certificate. A Boolean formula with n variables and m clauses is satisfiable when some assignment makes it true; the assignment is the certificate and checking it costs O(m) steps for clauses of bounded length (as in 3-SAT), and O(total formula length) in general. A problem is NP-complete when it lies in NP and every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time. Satisfiability (SAT) is the standard example.

BQP is the quantum class: bounded-error quantum polynomial time. A decision problem is in BQP when a polynomial-size quantum circuit decides it with error at most 1/3. In words, measuring the output qubit gives the correct answer with probability at least 2/3. The circuit family must be uniform: a classical polynomial-time algorithm must produce the circuit for each input length n.
Pr[correct] ≥ 1 − ε, with ε ≤ 1/3 and circuit size ≤ poly(n)
blocks.where: Pr[correct] is the probability that measuring the circuit's output qubit equals the true answer; ε is the allowed error; poly(n) means at most c·n<sup>k</sup> for fixed constants c and k, with n the number of input bits.

blocks.text: The 1/3 is not special. Running the circuit 2r+1 times and taking the majority answer pushes the error down to roughly e<sup>−cr</sup>, so any fixed error below 1/2 describes the same class. Some syllabi call BQP bounded quantum polynomial time; both names mean this one class.

sections.h3: The inclusion ladder, and the rung we cannot place

blocks.text: P ⊆ BQP. Classical reversible gates such as Toffoli are quantum gates. A quantum circuit can therefore replay any polynomial-size classical circuit gate by gate and measure at the end. Everything easy classically is easy quantumly.

BQP ⊆ PSPACE. PSPACE holds the problems solvable with polynomial memory, with no limit on running time. A classical machine can compute one output amplitude of a poly-size circuit by summing over all computational paths that lead to it. That sum is exponentially long but needs only polynomial working memory, so every BQP problem sits inside PSPACE. Quantum computers are fast, not unlimited.
The classical ladder P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE is standard. BQP crosses NP in a way nobody has pinned down: neither BQP ⊆ NP nor NP ⊆ BQP has been proved.
P ⊆ BQP ⊆ PSPACE   and   P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE
blocks.where: P is polynomial-time classical; NP is polynomial-time verifiable; BQP is bounded-error quantum polynomial time; PSPACE is polynomial memory, unlimited time. The relation between BQP and NP is unknown.

sections.h3: Factoring is not NP-complete, and Grover is only quadratic

blocks.text: Shor's algorithm decides in polynomial time whether N has a factor below a given bound; this is the decision version of factoring. So factoring ∈ BQP. Factoring is also in NP, because a factor is a short certificate. It is not known to be NP-complete, and most researchers believe it is not.

The gap matters. If factoring were NP-complete, then BQP would contain one NP-complete problem. Since every NP problem reduces to it quickly, all of NP would land inside BQP. Nobody expects such a collapse from a problem with the tight algebraic structure of factoring.

For NP-complete problems the best general quantum tool is Grover search. If the search space has N = 2<sup>n</sup> candidates for n Boolean variables, Grover finds a marked one in about (π/4)√N oracle calls. Chapter 4.8 shows that no black-box quantum algorithm can do much better.

blocks.where: n is the number of Boolean variables; 2<sup>n</sup> is the number of candidate assignments; π/4 ≈ 0.785 is the constant from the optimal Grover iteration count.

blocks.text: The exponent halves; it does not vanish. A quadratic speedup buys real time on small instances, but it does not move an NP-complete problem into BQP. Advertisements that a quantum computer "solves NP-complete problems" usually hide this one step.

figure.caption: Known inclusions are drawn as solid arrows and factoring is placed inside BQP; the dashed arrow between BQP and NP is a relation no one has settled.

spec.aria: A graph of complexity classes shows P inside BQP and NP, BQP and NP inside PSPACE, NP-complete inside NP, factoring placed in BQP, and a dashed unknown relation between BQP and NP.

examples.question: A Boolean satisfiability instance has n = 50 variables. Compare classical brute-force search with Grover's algorithm. Give the number of assignments classically checked and the number of oracle calls Grover needs, and say whether either count is polynomial in n.
steps: The number of candidate assignments is N = 2^n = 2^50.
Compute the classical count: 2^50 = 1,125,899,906,842,624. This is about 1.13×10^15 checks in the worst case.
Grover needs about (π/4)·√N oracle calls. Here √N = √(2^50) = 2^25 = 33,554,432.
Compare the growth rates. The classical count is 2^n and the quantum count is 2^(n/2). Doubling n squares both numbers, so the quantum count stays exponential in n.
Conclusion: the speedup factor is large on this instance (about 4×10^7) but it is only quadratic, so n = 50 still needs tens of millions of oracle calls and n = 200 is hopeless for either method.
examples.answer: Classical brute force checks 1,125,899,906,842,624 assignments while Grover needs about 26,353,589 oracle calls, a quadratic speedup that is still exponential in n.
examples.check:
import math
n = 50
N = 2**n
grover = (math.pi/4) * math.sqrt(N)
print(N)
print(round(grover))

traps: BQP is a class of decision problems with bounded error, not a label for anything a quantum computer can attempt. Saying "BQP includes all quantum algorithms" is wrong.
Shor puts factoring in BQP. Factoring is not known to be NP-complete, so this says nothing about NP-complete problems. Examiners test exactly this confusion.
Grover reduces 2^n to 2^(n/2). The exponent halves; it does not disappear. Writing "Grover solves NP-complete problems in polynomial time" loses all marks.
NP does not stand for "not polynomial". It means nondeterministic polynomial time, and equivalently, polynomial-time verifiability of a YES answer.
The relation between BQP and NP is open in both directions. Any answer that presents BQP ⊆ NP or NP ⊆ BQP as a proved theorem is wrong, because both are open.

quiz.q: Define BQP in one sentence, including the error bound.
quiz.a: BQP is the class of decision problems decided by a uniform polynomial-size quantum circuit whose measured output is correct with probability at least 2/3, that is, error at most 1/3.

quiz.q: State two proved inclusions that involve BQP.

quiz.a: Classical reversible gates such as Toffoli are quantum gates, so a polynomial-size classical circuit can be made reversible and then simulated by a quantum circuit. The quantum circuit has size at most a constant factor larger than the classical circuit (after making the classical gates reversible), and it is measured at the end.

quiz.q: Why is the exact value 1/3 in the BQP definition not important?
quiz.a: Repeating the circuit 2r+1 times and taking the majority drops the error to about e^(−cr). So any fixed bound below 1/2 gives the same class.

quiz.q: A SAT instance has n = 40 variables. How many assignments does classical brute force check in the worst case, and about how many oracle calls does Grover need?
A classmate says: "Factoring is hard, Shor factors, so quantum computers will crack NP-complete problems." Identify the two errors.
quiz.a: First, factoring is not known to be NP-complete, so putting it in BQP does not put NP in BQP. Second, the only general quantum tool for NP-complete problems is Grover, which gives a quadratic speedup, still exponential in n.

quiz.q: What does BQP ⊆ PSPACE tell you about the limits of quantum computers?
quiz.a: Any problem a quantum computer can decide in polynomial time with bounded error can also be decided classically using polynomial memory, so quantum speedups never escape PSPACE.

quiz.q: Name one problem known to be in BQP and not known to be in P, and one problem in NP not known to be in BQP.
quiz.a: Factoring is in BQP and not known to be in P. Boolean satisfiability (or any NP-complete problem such as the travelling salesman decision problem) is in NP and not known to be in BQP.

beyond: Not for the exam. Exact relations between BQP and NP are settled only relative to oracles, and progress there is slow. A neighbouring class, QMA, is the quantum version of NP: a quantum proof checked by a quantum verifier, and it contains the local Hamiltonian problem. Researchers also study BQP with restricted gate sets, and complexity arguments are used to argue that quantum supremacy experiments cannot be efficiently simulated classically. Search next for "QMA", "quantum supremacy complexity argument" and "polynomial method lower bounds".
